alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an entirely different pericope (the Transfiguration narrative, Mark 9:2) while the Greek and Peshitta preserve Mark 9:1 (the saying about some not tasting death). This represents a complete textual divergence, likely due to misalignment in the input data rather than a genuine variant tradition.

Greek uses imperfect ἔλεγεν (simple verb); Peshitta employs periphrastic construction ܘܐܡܪ ܗܘܐ (participle + auxiliary), a common Syriac idiom for past progressive aspect. Both convey iterative or durative past action.

Peshitta inserts explicit subject pronoun ܐܢܐ ('I') after ܐܡܪ, making the speaker explicit where Greek relies on verbal inflection alone (λέγω, first-person singular). This is a typical Syriac clarifying expansion.

Greek conjunction ὅτι introducing indirect discourse is absent in Peshitta, which uses the relative particle ܕ (d-) prefixed to the following verb instead. This represents a syntactic difference in how the two languages mark subordination.

Greek uses adverb ὧδε + articular participle τῶν ἑστηκότων ('here of those standing'); Peshitta employs participial phrase ܕܩܝܡܝܢ ܬܢܢ ('who are standing here'), reversing word order. Both are semantically equivalent but syntactically distinct.

Greek relative pronoun οἵτινες ('who') is absent in Peshitta, which continues the participial construction without an additional relative marker. The Syriac ܕ (d-) prefix on the following negative serves this function.

Greek employs emphatic double negative οὐ μή (strongest negation in Koine); Peshitta uses simple negative ܕܠܐ (d-lā). While both express strong negation, the Greek construction is rhetorically more emphatic.

Greek uses ἕως ἂν (temporal conjunction + modal particle) to express indefinite future time; Peshitta employs simple ܥܕܡܐ (ʿdammā, 'until'). The Greek construction emphasizes contingency more explicitly.

Greek uses articular noun phrase τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ('the kingdom of God'); Peshitta employs construct state ܡܠܟܘܬܗ ܕܐܠܗܐ ('kingdom-his of-God'), with pronominal suffix on 'kingdom'. Both are standard constructions in their respective languages for expressing genitive relationships.
